name: Infrastructure as code
summary: Describe your infrastructure in files and let a tool build it.
howItWorks: Instead of clicking through a console, you declare resources (networks, databases, queues, permissions) in files kept in git. The tool compares that desired state with what exists, shows a plan of what it will create, change or destroy, and then calls the cloud APIs to apply it. Environments become reproducible, changes get code review, and the history lives in version control.
analogy: An architect’s blueprint. Hand the same drawings to any builder and you get the same house, and every change starts as a revision on paper.
useWhen: Keeping dev, staging and production identical
Reviewing infrastructure changes like code, with a plan preview
avoidWhen: Editing tool-managed resources by hand in the console; that creates drift
Treating the state file casually; store it safely and lock it
example: A pull request adds a queue and lets a function read from it. CI runs `terraform plan`, the reviewer sees “2 to add, 1 to change”, and merging applies it to staging and then production.

providers.oss: Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi; SST for full-stack apps on AWS and Cloudflare; Packer for machine images; HCP Waypoint as a self-service portal on Terraform

source: # $ terraform plan  ->  Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

diagram.caption: Each change to the code produces a plan, and the cloud API creates or updates exactly the resources that plan lists.

story: In 1993 Mark Burgess, a theoretical physicist at the University of Oslo, wrote CFEngine to automate the upkeep of Unix machines. Fixes made by hand or with shell scripts grew cumbersome and haphazard, and every flavour of Unix needed its own. CFEngine took another approach: describe in one file how every host should be configured, and let the tool check and repair each machine as many times as needed, without human intervention.

That idea of declared, repeatable configuration spread with the growth of server fleets: Luke Kanies started Puppet in 2005 and Chef was released in 2009, both managing what was installed and configured on machines. Cloud computing then made the machines themselves, along with networks, load balancers and databases, something you could create with an API call. On February 25, 2011, AWS launched CloudFormation, which builds a whole stack of resources from one JSON template in the right order. Its launch post compared a template to a baking recipe, where precise ratios give “repeatable, high-quality results every time”.

CloudFormation only covered AWS. Terraform, released in 2014, used the same declarative approach across many clouds through provider plugins, with a plan step that shows exactly what will change before anything does. When HashiCorp moved Terraform to a source-available licence in 2023, its community fork OpenTofu was taken in by the Linux Foundation, and in 2025 it joined the CNCF.

choices.choice: Declare the desired end state, not the steps
choices.why: Step-by-step scripts break when a machine isn’t in the state the script expects. Describing the end result lets the tool work out what to change, and running it again changes nothing, which is what makes it safe to repeat.

choices.choice: Keep the definitions in version control
choices.why: Infrastructure files can be reviewed, diffed and rolled back like application code, and the same template can create identical environments for development, testing and production.
With whole networks and databases at stake, Terraform shows a plan of every create, update and destroy and acts only on approval, so mistakes can be caught in review instead of in production.

timeline.text: Mark Burgess creates CFEngine at the University of Oslo
AWS CloudFormation launches in February with JSON templates
HashiCorp releases Terraform, cloud-agnostic, in July
Terraform relicensed; OpenTofu fork joins the Linux Foundation
